title: The History of Las Vegas
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck trace the history of Las Vegas from early Indigenous habitation and the Vegas spring, through Wuvi (Southern Paiute) use, the 1855 Mormon mission and fort, Octavius Decatur Gass's ranch, the railroad rivalry between William Clark and E. H. Harriman, the founding of the town and Clark County, Nevada's gambling laws, Guy McAfee and the Paradise strip, the 1940s-50s casino boom and mob involvement including Bugsy Siegel and the Flamingo, Howard Hughes's buyouts, and the 1970s-80s decline followed by Steve Wynn's Mirage. Ends with listener mail correcting a detail from the Teleisian Massacre episode.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show with banter about the episode's Old West theme and plan to cover Las Vegas history from Indigenous tribes forward.

segments.title: Early habitation and the Vegas spring
segments.summary: Chuck describes evidence of early habitation near Las Vegas and the spring that drew people to the area after it formed around eight thousand years ago.

segments.title: Wuvi people and the Old Spanish Trail
segments.summary: The Wuvi people, part of the Southern Paiute, lived around the spring as hunter-gatherers. Permanent settlement came later, and Las Vegas became a stop on the Old Spanish Trail trade route between Santa Fe and Los Angeles in 1829.

segments.title: Mexican territory and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
segments.summary: Las Vegas was part of Mexico until the Mexican-American War; the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred the territory to the United States. The 1849 Gold Rush increased traffic through the area.

segments.title: Mormon mission and fort
segments.summary: In 1855 Brigham Young sent William Bringhurst and about thirty people to build a fort and mission near Las Vegas. They baptized Paiute people, attempted farming, and found lead and set up a mine. The mission was abandoned because the spring could not sustain intensive agriculture, though the fort remains.

segments.title: Octavius Decatur Gass and the Las Vegas Ranch
segments.summary: Octavius Decatur Gass, a prefab house seller turned miner, acquired the Mormon fort with partners and turned it into a ranch and rest stop, growing grapes for wine. Later, after territorial boundary changes, Gass lost political standing, and a freak weather event wiped out his crop, forcing him to hand the ranch to Archibald Stuart.

segments.title: Mining boom and need for a railroad
segments.summary: Mining in the Eldorado Canyon area boomed with copper, lead, gold, and silver, but without a railroad, ore moved slowly by armed freight wagons.

segments.title: Railroad rivalry and the founding of Las Vegas town
segments.summary: William Clark and E. H. Harriman, head of Union Pacific, fought over railroad routes, and Clark eventually sold his interest to Harriman while focusing on building a town. J. T. McWilliams, an African American surveyor, built a rival town on the west side of the tracks. Clark bought the Las Vegas Rancho and subdivided it into lots in 1904-1905.

segments.title: Clark County naming and William Clark's legacy
segments.summary: Clark County is named after William Clark, whom Mark Twain criticized and who bribed the Montana legislature to become senator, prompting the Seventeenth Amendment.

segments.title: Early Nevada gambling laws
segments.summary: Gambling was outlawed in 1861, legalized in 1869, made illegal again in 1909, and wide open gambling was legalized in 1931 during the Depression, though Nevada still has no lottery.

segments.title: Fremont Street and the Golden Gate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Golden Gate casino, opened in 1906, and the Fremont Street Experience with its light canopy and the Vegas Vic sign.

segments.title: Guy McAfee and the Paradise strip
segments.summary: Former LAPD vice squad commander Guy McAfee moved to Las Vegas and bought the Golden Nugget and the Paradise Club. He set up an unincorporated area called Paradise outside city limits, which became the location of the Strip.

segments.title: Early Strip hotels and Thomas Hall
segments.summary: Thomas Hall opened El Rancho Vegas in 1941 as a self-contained resort with a pool, restaurants, and casino.

segments.title: Casino boom of the 1940s and 1950s
segments.summary: Hosts list casinos and events of the fifties: the Desert Inn, El Dorado Club and Binion's Horseshoe, the Riviera, Liberace's residency, the Stardust, and the first wedding chapels. They note about ten to eleven casinos were built in the fifties, many tied to the mafia.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode sponsor break.

segments.title: Bugsy Siegel and the Flamingo
segments.summary: Hosts describe Benjamin Siegelbaum's rise from New York bootlegging and Murder Inc. to Los Angeles, then his involvement in building the Flamingo in Las Vegas after Billy Wilkerson's loan. They discuss the film Bugsy and the hotel's costly opening and reopening in 1947.

segments.title: Bugsy Siegel's assassination and theories
segments.summary: Siegel was shot in June 1947 at Virginia Hill's Los Angeles home. The traditional view is a mob hit. Bernie Sendler disputed this, suggesting a Hill family member, and the hosts discuss his reasoning.

segments.title: Sin City and McCarran Airport
segments.summary: Sin City nickname, from a 1963 book, grows out of Vegas' reputation for gambling, marriage, divorce, and legal sex work. McCarran Airport opened in 1962, boosting visitors.

segments.title: Howard Hughes and corporate gaming licenses
segments.summary: Howard Hughes bought casinos from the mob and pushed the Gaming Commission to change corporate ownership rules so only key executives needed background checks, opening the industry to Wall Street corporations.

segments.title: Seventies and eighties decline and family-friendly shift
segments.summary: Vegas lost its glitz in the seventies and eighties, then Steve Wynn built the Mirage and attracted families, reshaping the city into an ultra-luxury destination.

segments.title: Closing wrap-up of history
segments.summary: Chuck wraps up the history, noting the episode went past the late eighties and nineties and recommending further reading and visits.

segments.title: Listener mail: Teleisian Massacre correction
segments.summary: A listener from Cleveland writes about a detail in the Teleisian Massacre episode, the gasoline and the Julian Carlton grave, and a Find a Grave joke. Chuck responds.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh give the mailing address and sign off with the show's production credit.
